q: In Hazzard's discussion of the free-radical theory of aging, which process links free-radical production to damage of cellular macromolecules?
o: Lipid peroxidation damages cellular proteins and nucleic acids
Lipid peroxidation protects cellular proteins against oxidative injury
Free-radical production reduces lipid peroxidation within aging cells
Free-radical production preserves nucleic acids by increasing caloric intake
explanation:
Free radicals can initiate oxidation of membrane lipids. **Lipid peroxidation damages cellular macromolecules**, linking reactive molecules to injury in the free-radical theory of aging.

**A. Lipid peroxidation causes injury.** Oxidative reactions and their products damage lipids, proteins and nucleic acids.
**B. Protection of proteins.** The reactive products can injure proteins rather than shield them.
**C. Reduced lipid peroxidation.** Free radicals initiate and propagate oxidation of susceptible lipids.
**D. Preserved nucleic acids with higher intake.** The theory proposes increased oxidative injury with greater radical production, not protection through increased caloric intake.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1274.

q: A 77-year-old man with chronic kidney disease and asymptomatic, non-life-threatening hyperkalemia is assessed in an outpatient clinic. Which approach addresses reversible contributors as described in Hazzard?
o: Shift potassium into cells while deferring review of contributing medications
Review contributing medications, hydration status, and reversible kidney dysfunction
Give intravenous calcium to remove the excess potassium from the body
Give sodium bicarbonate while deferring assessment of acid-base status
explanation:
Stable, non-life-threatening hyperkalemia in chronic kidney disease often has a reversible contributor. **Review medications, hydration and any recent fall in renal function** to identify why potassium clearance has declined.

**A. Shift potassium first.** Redistribution can lower serum potassium temporarily while the precipitating medication continues to act.
**B. Review reversible factors.** Stopping a contributing drug or correcting volume depletion addresses the mechanism of potassium retention.
**C. IV calcium for removal.** Calcium protects the myocardium without lowering serum or total-body potassium.
**D. Bicarbonate without acid-base assessment.** Accompanying metabolic acidosis is a reason to consider bicarbonate, so acid-base status matters.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1271.
ref: Hazzard Ch 82 — AGING OF THE KIDNEY

q: A patient with chronic kidney disease takes spironolactone and develops non-life-threatening hyperkalemia. Which approach addresses a reversible contributor to the potassium elevation?
o: Add another inhibitor of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system
Identify and stop a medication contributing to hyperkalemia
Add a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug to improve clearance
Continue the medication and defer evaluation until ECG changes appear
explanation:
Spironolactone reduces aldosterone-mediated potassium excretion. For stable hyperkalemia, **identify and hold the contributing drug** while assessing renal function and following the potassium concentration.

**A. Add a renin–angiotensin inhibitor.** Further suppression of aldosterone signaling can worsen potassium retention.
**B. Stop a contributing drug.** Holding spironolactone removes a reversible impediment to urinary potassium excretion.
**C. Add an NSAID.** NSAIDs can worsen renal perfusion and potassium handling.
**D. Wait for ECG changes.** Clinically important hyperkalemia can precede ECG abnormalities, so a normal tracing cannot justify deferral.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1271.
ref: Hazzard Ch 82 — AGING OF THE KIDNEY

q: A patient with chronic kidney disease requests treatment for joint pain. Which prescribing principle is emphasized in Hazzard’s chapter on the aging kidney?
o: Prefer NSAIDs as a means of preserving the patient’s residual kidney function
Choose medication doses without accounting for the extent of renal excretion
Avoid potential renal toxins and adjust renally excreted medication dosing
Choose dosing intervals without accounting for the extent of renal excretion
explanation:
In CKD, **avoid nephrotoxic exposures and adapt renally cleared medicines to kidney function**. Check changes in renal function, interacting drugs and whether a dose or interval adjustment is needed.

**A. Prefer NSAIDs for renal preservation.** Systemic NSAIDs can impair renal perfusion and worsen kidney function.
**B. Ignore renal excretion when dosing.** Accumulation can cause toxicity, especially with predominantly renally cleared drugs.
**C. Avoid toxins and adjust doses.** This addresses both further kidney injury and excessive drug exposure.
**D. Ignore renal excretion when setting intervals.** Lengthening the interval is one valid adjustment for some drugs.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, Ch 82, p. 1275.
ref: Hazzard Ch 82 — AGING OF THE KIDNEY

q: An older woman with reduced renal clearance is taking a medication excreted by the kidney. Which principle should guide a safety review of the prescription?
o: Consider increasing the dose to compensate for reduced kidney function.
Consider adjusting the dose amount and the frequency of administration.
Consider shortening dose intervals to compensate for reduced renal clearance.
Consider adjusting for the clinical response while disregarding renal clearance.
explanation:
Reduced renal clearance prolongs exposure to a renally eliminated drug. **Reconsider both the dose and the dosing interval** to prevent accumulation while maintaining benefit.

**A. Increase the dose.** More drug per dose raises exposure when elimination is already slow.
**B. Adjust dose and frequency.** A lower dose, longer interval or both may be appropriate depending on the drug and measured renal function.
**C. Shorten the interval.** Closer doses allow even less time for clearance between administrations.
**D. Use response alone.** Toxicity may develop before a clinical change signals excessive exposure.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 303, 1275.
ref: Hazzard Ch 82 — AGING OF THE KIDNEY

q: An 80-year-old man with renal failure and severe hyperkalemia develops a conduction abnormality on ECG. Which treatment provides immediate myocardial protection by stabilizing the cell membrane while potassium-lowering treatment is also planned?
o: Administer intravenous calcium gluconate
Administer insulin by the intravenous route
Administer an intravenous loop diuretic
Administer an oral ion-exchange resin
explanation:
Severe hyperkalemia with ECG conduction changes requires **intravenous calcium for immediate myocardial protection**. Calcium does not lower potassium, so start potassium-shifting and removal measures as appropriate.

**A. IV calcium gluconate.** It rapidly antagonizes the membrane effects of potassium. Monitor the ECG and reassess the response.
**B. IV insulin.** With glucose management, it shifts potassium intracellularly but does not replace calcium for immediate membrane stabilization.
**C. IV loop diuretic.** It can increase urinary potassium loss if renal function and urine output permit.
**D. Oral ion-exchange resin.** Its effect is too slow to protect against an imminent arrhythmia.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1271. UK Kidney Association, Management of Hyperkalaemia in Adults, 2026.
ref: Hazzard Ch 82 — AGING OF THE KIDNEY

q: An 81-year-old man has severe hyperkalemia with bradycardia and marked conduction delay. What immediate effect does Hazzard attribute to intravenous calcium gluconate in this situation?
o: An immediate increase in urinary potassium loss through enhanced excretion by the kidneys.
An immediate redistribution of extracellular potassium into cells through increased cellular potassium uptake.
An immediate reduction in body potassium stores through enhanced intestinal elimination of potassium.
An immediate stabilization of myocardial cell membranes with a transient reduction in cardiac risk.
explanation:
Severe hyperkalemia impairs cardiac conduction. With bradycardia and marked conduction delay, IV calcium provides **immediate, temporary myocardial membrane stabilization** while potassium-lowering treatment begins.

**A. Urinary potassium loss.** Diuresis can remove potassium when kidney function permits. Calcium has no such renal effect.
**B. Intracellular shift.** Insulin and beta agonists shift potassium into cells. Calcium primarily protects cardiac excitability.
**C. Intestinal elimination.** Potassium binders remove potassium through the gut and do not give immediate membrane protection.
**D. Myocardial stabilization.** Calcium rapidly reduces electrical toxicity, but serum potassium still needs separate treatment.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1271.
ref: Hazzard Ch 82 — AGING OF THE KIDNEY

q: An older adult taking spironolactone starts trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Which electrolyte risk does Hazzard emphasize for this combination?
o: Development of significant hyperkalemia during treatment
Development of hypokalemia from the combined medications
A sustained potassium decrease requiring preventive supplementation
Potassium loss that offsets the effect of spironolactone
explanation:
Trimethoprim and spironolactone both impair distal potassium secretion. Together they can cause **marked hyperkalemia**, particularly when renal reserve is reduced.

**A. Hyperkalemia.** The two potassium-retaining effects add together, making monitoring important.
**B. Hypokalemia.** Neither drug produces the potassium wasting that would explain a low concentration here.
**C. Preventive potassium replacement.** Supplementation adds to potassium retention and can worsen the interaction.
**D. Offsetting potassium loss.** Trimethoprim reinforces, rather than counteracts, spironolactone's potassium-sparing effect.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1271.
ref: Hazzard Ch 82 — AGING OF THE KIDNEY

q: מה מאפיין פיזיולוגיה של הזדקנות הכליה?
o: פרוטאינוריה
זרימת הדם לכליה עולה
ירידה בנפח הכליה
עלייה בקראטינין בדם
explanation:
Normal renal aging includes loss of cortical tissue and functioning nephrons. **Kidney volume decreases**, even though serum creatinine can appear reassuring when muscle mass also falls.

**A. Proteinuria.** Persistent protein loss suggests renal disease and warrants assessment.
**B. Increased renal blood flow.** Renal perfusion generally falls with age, reducing reserve.
**C. Decreased renal volume.** Loss of parenchyma reduces the size of the kidney.
**D. Increased serum creatinine.** Reduced creatinine generation can offset reduced filtration, so a rise is not a necessary feature of normal aging.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1267–1269.

q: Why can a rising serum creatinine be pathological even when it remains near the laboratory normal range?
o: A value at the upper limit of normal excludes significant loss of renal function
Serum creatinine should rise with normal aging and need not affect renal drug dosing
Creatinine production increases as muscle mass falls, so a rising level is normal aging
Muscle loss reduces creatinine production, so serum creatinine should remain relatively constant
explanation:
Aging often reduces muscle mass and creatinine production at the same time as filtration declines. **A rise above a patient’s baseline can therefore signal renal dysfunction even within the laboratory reference range**.

**A. Upper-normal value excludes disease.** A low-muscle-mass patient can have impaired filtration at an apparently normal creatinine.
**B. A rise is expected and irrelevant to dosing.** Changes in kidney function can alter drug clearance and warrant assessment.
**C. Muscle loss increases creatinine production.** Less skeletal muscle generally produces less creatinine.
**D. Lower production offsets declining filtration.** Serum creatinine may remain fairly stable with aging, making trends and renal estimates more informative than the reference range alone.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, Ch 82, p. 1268.

q: Is proteinuria an expected consequence of normal human aging?
o: No - proteinuria is pathological and requires a full work-up in older humans
No - proteinuria needs no work-up when creatinine stays in its normal range
Yes - the normal decline in GFR makes proteinuria expected in older humans
Yes - proteinuria is normal in aging humans as it is in rats
explanation:
GFR commonly declines with age, but filtration rate and urinary protein loss measure different aspects of kidney health. **Proteinuria warrants evaluation in an older adult**, even with a normal creatinine.

**A. Investigate proteinuria.** It can signal glomerular or other renal disease independently of the estimated GFR.
**B. Normal creatinine needs no workup.** Preserved filtration does not exclude abnormal protein passage into urine.
**C. Expected as GFR falls.** A lower filtration rate alone does not explain pathological protein leakage.
**D. Normal in rats and humans.** Age-associated proteinuria in rodent models cannot be assumed to be physiologic in humans.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1269.

q: As GFR declines, how does potassium fractional excretion differ in older versus younger adults?
o: The fractional excretion of potassium does not rise as much as in young individuals
It rises more than in young individuals because aldosterone levels increase
A smaller fractional-excretion rise usually makes unstressed serum potassium abnormal
The fractional-excretion rise is similar in younger and older adults despite declining GFR
explanation:
Remaining nephrons increase fractional potassium excretion as GFR falls. **Older adults have a smaller compensatory rise** than younger adults, partly owing to reduced aldosterone activity or responsiveness.

**A. Smaller increase.** Reduced secretory reserve becomes important during a potassium load or a medication change.
**B. Larger aldosterone-driven increase.** Diminished aldosterone activity or resistance works in the opposite direction.
**C. Usually abnormal baseline potassium.** Potassium can remain normal without a challenge when filtration is relatively preserved.
**D. Equal responses across ages.** Similar resting potassium levels can conceal a difference in adaptive reserve.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1270.

q: Does absence of typical ECG changes exclude dangerous hyperkalemia?
o: No - absence of ECG findings does not make hyperkalemia erroneous or insignificant
No - a given potassium level usually produces the same ECG pattern across patients
Yes - the classic sequence of ECG changes is the usual pattern of dangerous hyperkalemia
Yes - an absent ECG pattern generally establishes that the potassium result is erroneous
explanation:
Hyperkalemia impairs cardiac conduction, but ECG sensitivity is limited. **A normal tracing cannot exclude dangerous hyperkalemia** or invalidate an elevated potassium measurement.

**A. Take the potassium seriously.** Cardiac toxicity varies among patients, and typical changes can be subtle or absent.
**B. Same level, same tracing.** Identical potassium concentrations can produce very different electrical findings.
**C. Classic ECG sequence.** Patients do not reliably progress through every textbook stage.
**D. Assume laboratory error.** A suspected sampling artifact requires prompt verification. The ECG alone cannot identify it.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1271.

q: What makes podocyte loss important in the proposed sclerosis mechanism?
o: Damaged podocytes are postmitotic cells without the capacity for replacement
Complete glomerular sclerosis preserves the affected nephron and its filtration capacity
Podocyte detachment maintains basement-membrane coverage and protects against glomerular sclerosis
Podocytes multiply in proportion to the enlargement of the glomerular tuft
explanation:
**Mature podocytes have very limited capacity to replace lost cells**. As the glomerular tuft enlarges, remaining podocytes must cover more basement membrane. Detachment exposes segments to adhesion and sclerosis.

**A. Postmitotic podocytes.** Limited regenerative capacity makes cell loss a critical event in the proposed pathway.
**B. Sclerosis preserves filtration.** Complete glomerulosclerosis eliminates filtration by the affected nephron.
**C. Detachment preserves coverage.** Detachment instead leaves areas of basement membrane uncovered.
**D. Proliferation matches tuft growth.** Surviving cells may hypertrophy, but they cannot reliably expand in number to match the surface area.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, Ch 82, p. 1272.

q: Does the chapter establish protein restriction as prevention of normal human kidney aging?
o: No - protein restriction tends to worsen symptoms in established uremia
Yes - lower-protein vegetarians had better-preserved kidney function than meat eaters
Yes - animal studies establish prevention of normal human kidney aging
No - evidence supports uremic symptom reduction, not prevention of human kidney aging
explanation:
Protein restriction can reduce nitrogenous waste and symptoms in established uremia. **It has not been shown to prevent normal human kidney aging**.

**A. Worsens uremic symptoms.** Reducing protein intake can relieve symptoms of established uremia.
**B. Better filtration in vegetarians.** The vegetarian and nonvegetarian comparison found no difference in kidney function.
**C. Prevention shown in animals.** Effects on animal kidney aging do not demonstrate a protective effect in people.
**D. Symptom relief, uncertain prevention.** Relief of uremic symptoms in established disease cannot demonstrate preservation of healthy aging kidneys.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1274.
